paragraphs: Scope and boundaries: This page covers only O*NET 39-9011.01 Nannies (who care for children in private households). It excludes related occupations such as teaching in preschool institutions, childcare institution management, and general domestic services. Employment arrangements, working hours, rest, and safety responsibilities when minors are present depend on employment contracts and local law.

How to assess fit: Conduct a paper exercise with an entirely fictional child and family scenario. Write a daily schedule, safety checks, parent-handover points, and three escalation routes for exceptions. Do not use real child or family information.

Potential fit: Willingness to spend time with children over the long term, follow agreed routines and rules, notice safety details, and communicate clearly with parents. Note: If prolonged continuous presence, unclear household boundaries, or responsibility for minors' safety is difficult to accept, compare related directions first.

Note: These are editorially designed paper exercises. They involve no real childcare, first-aid treatment, or employment relationship and grant no occupational or practice authorization. Matters involving child safety, first aid, and labor relationships must refer back to employers and local law.

The official definition of Nannies (O*NET 39-9011.01) is to care for children in private households and provide parents with support and professional assistance in meeting children's physical, emotional, intellectual, and social needs. Duties may include meal planning and preparation, laundry and clothing care, play activities and outings, discipline, intellectual stimulation, language activities, and transportation. The scope excludes institutional preschool teaching and childcare institution management.

entries: Daily care and safety: Teach children safe behavior, remove hazards, establish rules and boundaries, and administer first aid or cardiopulmonary resuscitation when necessary.
Habits and routines: Instruct and assist children in healthy and personal habits such as eating, resting, and toileting, and arrange rest periods and naps.
Activities and intellectual stimulation: Organize age-appropriate games, reading, and crafts; model social behavior and encourage concern for others.
Health observation and medical assistance: Observe unusual behavior, take temperatures, administer medication as directed, and accompany children to medical visits or provide transportation.
Housework and shopping: Perform cleaning and household tasks related to childcare, and purchase food, clothing, and other necessities.
Parent communication and records: Regularly discuss children's activities and development with parents, document play, eating, and routines, and assist with family schedules.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): 84% of respondents work in very close physical proximity, 81% have face-to-face discussions daily, 80% work more than 40 hours per week, 71% report constant contact with others, 64% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting daily, 60% report considerable decision-making freedom, 56% stand more than half the time, 52% make decisions daily, and 50% work in enclosed vehicles or operate enclosed equipment daily. 44% consider the consequences of error extremely serious, 40% report very high responsibility for others' health and safety, 40% encounter noise daily, 40% work outdoors in all weather once a week or more, 32% kneel, crouch, stoop, or bend more than half the time, and 40% walk or run more than half the time.

Key capabilities: Continuously observe children's condition and respond promptly to exceptions, organize daily routines as agreed, clearly hand over facts to parents, and understand basic safety protection and first aid. Customer and personal service and education and training knowledge is needed, along with patience and responsibility.

Preparation and training: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zones 1—2 (SVP below 6.0), usually requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, though some positions may have no requirement. Related experience ranges from little or moderate experience to several months, and on-the-job training from a few days to a year. The occupational page publishes no training-program count or specific certification list; actual requirements depend on employers and local rules.

Professional judgment: Key judgments concern children's immediate safety, conflicts between parent agreements and current circumstances, clear authorization for medication or medical care, and whom to contact about exceptions. When uncertain, protect the child first and contact parents or emergency services.

Main outputs: Daily records suitable for handover (eating, routines, activities, and exceptions), communication and agreement records with parents, and household and shopping tasks completed as arranged by the employer.

Boundaries with related occupations: Nannies focus on daily childcare in private households; preschool teaching on curricula and group teaching; childcare institution management on institutional operations and staff management; and general domestic services on household affairs not primarily centered on childcare.

Conclusion: Nannies' core outputs are daily childcare in private households and records suitable for handover. Preschool teachers focus on institutional curricula and group teaching; early childhood education managers on institutional operations and staff management; domestic service workers on household affairs and cleaning; and childcare center workers on group care in institutions. These relationships serve only as comparisons and do not imply automatic transitions or mutual recognition of qualifications.
Comparisons draw on the official O*NET 39-9011.01 description and tasks and the O*NET profiles of related occupations. They are editorial syntheses, not job recommendations.
Comparison dimensions: This page compares core work and outputs, key differences from nannies, and the preferences each direction may suit, to help assess career preferences.

Difference from Preschool Teachers: Nannies provide daily care for one or a few children in private households. Preschool teachers organize group instruction by curriculum and class and take responsibility for learning assessment.

If you prefer institutional curricula and group teaching, compare preschool teachers; if institutional operations and staff management, compare education administrators; if services centered on household affairs and cleaning, compare domestic service workers; if clinical support for child health and care, compare childcare-related health occupations.

People caring for children at home: Establish fundamentals in safety checks, daily routines, and handover records before considering tools. AI can support information searches and record organization, but judgments of children's condition and safety responses remain your own tasks.
Do not use generated content as a basis for care. Child safety, dietary restrictions, and medication requirements must follow parents' written instructions and professional advice.

Caregivers working with parents: Use AI for activity ideas, draft menus, and record organization. Judgments involving children's health, medication, and emergencies still require confirmation by you and the parents.

Editorial trial suggestion: Check information/record candidates item by item. Actual acceleration effects have not been obtained; do not submit children's names, photos, health information, or home addresses to unauthorized services.

Experienced caregivers: Use AI for activity plans, shopping lists, and family schedule organization. You and parents confirm discipline methods, unusual child conditions, and parent communication wording.
Tools do not change responsibility: Caregivers still carry responsibility for child safety, emergency recognition, and accurate handover.

Employers and household managers: Define permitted tools, the scope of child information that may be processed, and recordkeeping requirements, and specify matters requiring immediate contact with parents or emergency services.

Insufficient evidence: No national occupational wages for nannies in China obtained. The five 2024 human resources and social security enterprise-employee wage percentiles for the resident service workers occupational subgroup are broad references only, not substitutes for direct household employment or the detailed nanny category.

Scope comparison: The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security's Enterprise Remuneration Survey Information (2024) publishes wage levels by occupational subgroup and does not separately identify nannies.

The 2024 human resources and social security enterprise survey reports five annual wage percentiles for resident service workers of 30100/38400/50100/66400/88000 yuan, covering many enterprise resident-service positions, not direct employment by private households or self-employment. Cash settlement itself is not an exclusion criterion.

The five 2024 human resources and social security enterprise-employee wage percentiles for the resident service workers occupational subgroup are broad references only, not substitutes for direct household employment or the detailed nanny category.

O*NET displays 2025 BLS OEWS national median wages of $34,980/year and $16.82/hour on this occupation's page. The original page labels wages and employment as covering the combined occupation Childcare Workers, not a separate value for 39-9011.01, and they do not represent starting pay, senior-position pay, or individual rates.

National percentiles under the same combined scope are: 10th percentile $24,260/year, 25th percentile $29,360/year, 75th percentile $38,570/year, and 90th percentile $46,010/year (corresponding hourly wages of $11.66, $14.12, $18.55, and $22.12).
Percentiles and medians all use the 2025 BLS OEWS national scope (combined occupation) and cannot be directly compared across years, regions, or occupations.

The 80% of O*NET nanny respondents working more than 40 hours is work-context information. 2025 OEWS covers the Childcare Workers group, excluding private-household employees and the self-employed. It is not wages for live-in or commuting nannies employed by private households; cash payment itself is not an exclusion criterion. Do not use that percentage to infer live-in earnings from group annual wages.

2025 OEWS covers the Childcare Workers group, excluding private-household employees and the self-employed. It is not wages for live-in or commuting nannies employed by private households; cash payment itself is not an exclusion criterion. Percentiles are not starting pay or personal net income; check actual hours and room-and-board contracts.
Check actual compensation by specific city, employer household, and contract terms; do not treat aggregate statistics as a promise of personal pay.

entries: The interest code S describes activity preferences: Helping, caring for, and teaching others. Compare these signals with real caregiving experience and parent feedback, rather than relying only on interest scores.
Compare these signals with specific work samples, parent feedback, and employer requirements.

Conscientiousness and emotional stability relate to following agreed routines and patiently handling unexpected situations, but do not equate to professional child-development knowledge or first-aid capabilities.
Extraversion/introversion does not determine safe competence. Child observation and handover are editorial observations; validity relative to assessments has not been established.
Type labels do not predict caregiving ability or safety judgment and cannot replace training and on-the-job experience.
Cognitive tests indicate only some reasoning and memory capabilities and cannot replace observing children's condition, following safety procedures, or handling unexpected situations.
Emotional awareness helps handle children's emotions and parent communication, but self-report scales are not grounds for hiring or occupational practice.

paragraphs: S describes preferences for helping, caring, and teaching activities, not ability, safety, or hiring. Care handover records can serve as editorial observations; comparative validity has not been established.
Exploratory evidence: Interest and personality frameworks support self-reflection, not occupational selection, hiring, or practice requirements.

Boundaries: This checklist is an editorial synthesis and does not replace first-aid and child-safety standards, employment and labor law, or requirements for young children's health and medication management. Specific responses and authorization depend on employer agreements, professional advice, and local law.

Key issues to assess in advance are child safety and accident risks, first-aid and medication authorization boundaries, physical strain from prolonged continuous presence, parent communication and unclear boundaries, and employment terms and rest arrangements. Exposure points differ across live-in, commuting, and accompanying travel settings.

Evidence scope: Work-context percentages reflect O*NET respondents (United States) and are not extrapolated to other regions. Wages and employment use the combined Childcare Workers scope labeled on the page. AI task exposure refers to the ILO 2025 global exposure index.
Affected roles and tasks: Personnel undertaking child supervision, transportation, outdoor activities, and household cleaning.

Editorial safety scenario: Continuous child observation is needed; error-consequence ratings are not accident incidence rates. No occupational child-accident incidence rate obtained; caregiver strain/employment disputes are not combined into the first card's accident outcomes.

Boundaries: Entry pathways and capability stages on this page are editorial compilations explaining a preparation sequence, not uniform industry ranks or a timetable guaranteeing promotion. Child safety, first-aid treatment, medication, and employment terms require confirmation under employer agreements and local law.
Can complete basic care routines under a trainer's or parent's instructions: Understand children's routines, diet, and safety requirements and document accurately.
Guided care
Can independently carry out daily routines, including meals, activities, naps, transportation, and exception reporting, and hand over to parents as agreed.
Independent care
Can arrange differentiated activities, handle conflicts and emotions in multiple-child or special-needs settings, and follow basic first-aid and safety procedures.
Care in complex settings
Can coordinate family schedules, shopping, and household tasks, establish stable communication with parents, and take responsibility for handover quality.

entries.answer: Nannies (O*NET 39-9011.01) care for children in private households, supporting parents in meeting children's physical, emotional, intellectual, and social needs. Typical work includes safety protection and first aid, meal and routine planning, games and outings, academic tutoring, housework and shopping, and regular parent communication and records.
entries.question: What exactly do nannies do?

entries.answer: Settings and core responsibilities differ: Nannies provide daily care for one or a few children in private households; preschool teachers organize group instruction by curriculum and class; childcare workers follow group-care standards in institutions.
entries.question: How does this occupation differ from preschool teachers and childcare workers?

entries.answer: Willingness to spend time with children over the long term, follow agreed routines and rules, notice safety details, and take caregiving responsibility. These are behavioral signals, not personality diagnoses.
entries.question: What kind of person may be better suited to being a nanny?

entries.answer: O*NET Job Zones are 1—2 (SVP below 6.0), usually requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, though some positions may have no requirement. Related experience and on-the-job training range from a few days to a year. Employers often prefer first-aid and CPR training; positions involving minors usually require background checks or references.

entries.answer: No. Interest and personality frameworks describe only activity preferences and general tendencies. They cannot determine caregiving ability or safety judgment. More reliable evidence includes care records, parent evaluations, and training certificates.

entries.answer: Evidence indicates that most occupations are more likely to be transformed than eliminated. Information searches, activity ideas, and record organization can be assisted, but childcare, safety judgment, and parent communication remain caregivers' responsibilities.

entries.answer: Primarily private households, in both live-in and commuting arrangements. O*NET industry distribution shows the occupation in healthcare and social assistance and other services (except public administration).

responsibility_steps.说明: Confirm children's dietary restrictions, allergies, medication, and emergency contacts, and verify parents' written agreements.

risk_rows.为什么重要: Accidental injuries to children can have serious consequences. O*NET reports that 44% of respondents consider error consequences extremely serious and 40% report very high responsibility for others' health and safety

personality_fit_block.heading: Fit signals, personality-tool boundaries, and practical use

questions.answer: Continual observation of children's condition, following agreed daily routines, safety protection and first-aid knowledge, and clear factual handover to parents.
questions.question: What capabilities do nannies mainly rely on?

questions.answer: No. S (Social) describes only preferences for helping and caring for others. Assess fit through caregiving experience and parent feedback.
questions.question: Can the S interest code determine whether I am suited to this career?

questions.answer: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zones 1—2, usually requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, though some positions have no requirement. Related experience and on-the-job training range from a few days to a year; actual requirements depend on employers.
questions.question: Can I enter without professional training?

questions.answer: Extraversion or introversion has little bearing. The key is whether you can provide patient care, consistently follow routines, and communicate promptly about safety issues.
questions.question: Are extraverts or introverts better suited?

questions.answer: JobZone1—2; 60% high school / 16% some college without a degree / 8% postsecondary certificates are occupational responses. The 752 training entries belong to the group; 3 certifications are in the US Nanny Association directory and do not replace first-aid capability or statutory conditions.
questions.question: What education, training, and qualifications are usually required for entry?

questions.answer: No. Assessments support self-exploration only and do not constitute evidence for hiring, occupational practice, or practice qualifications.
questions.question: Can assessment results serve as evidence for hiring or authorization?

questions.answer: The directory currently has 3 US Nanny Association certifications: Professional Nanny and Childcare, Newborn and Infant Care, and Nanny and Childcare. These are not Chinese entry requirements or uniform statutory permission. Check first aid/background screening by setting and jurisdiction.
questions.question: Is professional certification necessary?

questions.answer: Child safety responsibility, prolonged continuous presence, boundaries and communication with parents, and differences between settings such as live-in and commuting work.
questions.question: Which work factors have a major effect on fit?

questions.answer: Retain daily care records, parent evaluations, training and first-aid certificates, and verifiable handover and exception-handling records.
questions.question: How can I build reviewable professional evidence?

questions.answer: Use an entirely fictional child and family scenario to write a daily schedule, safety checks, and three escalation routes for exceptions. Then ask someone with caregiving experience for feedback against real standards.
questions.question: What kind of low-cost experiment should I try first?

signals.body: You continually attend to children's condition and safety details, consistently follow agreed routines and rules, and seek help promptly when exceptions or information gaps arise rather than deciding alone.
signals.label: Fit signals

signals.body: This occupation can be draining if you struggle with prolonged continuous presence, are unwilling to take responsibility for minors' safety, or find it difficult to communicate clearly with parents about rules and boundaries.
signals.label: Signals calling for caution

signals.body: Conduct a paper exercise using a fictional scenario. Write a daily schedule from waking to bedtime, five safety checks, parent-handover points, and escalation routes for three situations: a child is injured, a child develops a fever, and a parent's request conflicts with safety rules.
signals.label: Low-cost experiment

riasec_fit_block.fit_interest: Compare interest signals with real caregiving experience: Are you willing to spend time with children over the long term, follow agreed procedures, and take safety responsibility? Look beyond interest scores or self-labels.
riasec_fit_block.interest: O*NET assigns nannies the interest code S (Social): Preferences for helping, teaching, assisting, or serving others, involving social services, personal services, and teaching and education. Interests indicate only willingness to persist in such activities and cannot predict ability, hiring, or occupational qualifications.

eeat_signals.source: O*NET39-9011.01 nanny profile: 19 Tasks/S/work realities and education distribution 60/16/8. Wages / employment / industries / 752 training entries cover the Childcare Workers39-9011 group; 3 US Nanny Association certifications. The five 2025 wages of 24260/29360/34980/38570/46010 are correct, but OEWS excludes private-household employees/self-employment. Group 2025—2035 decline is 2%, net decrease 19900 / 150300 openings, with shares of 33/25/13/29. The five 2024 human resources and social security enterprise resident-service percentiles of 30100/38400/50100/66400/88000 are correct broad-scope figures. Opening the original page failed in this review; the full official table was obtained through search, without claiming a successful direct connection. China's Personal Information Protection Law Articles 28—31 and the Article 72 personal/household-affairs exception are separate.

components.work_context_block: Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): 84% of respondents work in very close physical proximity, 81% have face-to-face discussions daily, 80% work more than 40 hours per week, 71% have constant contact with others, 64% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting daily, 60% report considerable decision-making freedom, 56% stand more than half the time, 52% make decisions daily, and 50% work in enclosed vehicles or operate enclosed equipment daily. 44% consider error consequences extremely serious and 40% report very high responsibility for others' health and safety.

description.text: Nannies (O*NET 39-9011.01) care for children in private households, supporting parents in meeting children's physical, emotional, intellectual, and social needs. They arrange meals and routines, organize games and outings, help with homework, support habit formation and safety, and regularly communicate and hand over records to parents. This page uses only official sources to explain occupational scope, tasks, preparation requirements, Chinese and U.S. statistical scopes, and authorization boundaries.
